The fragmented lexicon continues to cascade, a digital avalanche of semantic debris that defies linear narrative structure. It is as if the collective unconscious of the internet has been distilled into a chaotic stream of consciousness, where the boundaries between code, commerce, and culture dissolve into a singular, pulsating noise. The word "Broadway" hangs suspended in the air, a neon sign flickering in the rain, while "fall" suggests a descent not just of leaves, but of order itself. Into this void, "eing" whispers, a fragment of a German verb, perhaps "eingeben," to input, to enter, to become part of the machine. The disturbance is palpable, an outbreak of meaning that refuses to be contained by traditional syntax. Unable to fib, the text confesses its own incoherence, recording the professor’s lecture on the nature of reality, where Halloween masks hide not faces, but the absence of identity. Commerce flows like blood through the veins of the city, bike lanes weaving through the gridlock of data packets.
